column3: States the immediate cause of the condemnation: attributing a child to the Merciful.
False attribution to God provides a relevant general frame for rejecting the claim of divine offspring.
Directly voices the claim that the Merciful has taken a child, which 19:92 declares impossible.
Rejects God taking a child and grounds the rejection in His decisive creative command.
Jesus' speech and human life cycle supply the immediate narrative context for the later rejection of sonship.
Taking disbelievers as allies concerns a different sense of taking and does not clarify divine sonship.
Tests the alleged child of the Merciful only to expose and negate the premise in the following declaration.
Its condemnation of fabricating a statement about God indirectly supports the rejection of an unsupported offspring claim.
What befits Solomon's kingdom is not a useful parallel to what befits the Merciful.
The paired denial of fitness and capacity gives a formal parallel to 19:92's structural impossibility.
Identifies Jesus as son of Mary amid the dispute that the ensuing anti-sonship passage resolves.
Taking one's precautions has no relevant connection to divine sonship.
Its hypothetical treatment of taking a child ends in God's oneness and absolute mastery, closely explaining the incompatibility.
Rejects the assertion that God has taken a child by affirming His self-sufficiency and ownership of all.
Taking revelations in mockery does not illuminate the divine-child attribution.
The statement that poetry does not befit the Prophet formally parallels the categorical suitability language of 19:92.
The later boast of wealth and children remains within the same passage but does not develop the claim about the Merciful.
Satan's claim to take a portion of servants is unrelated to divine offspring.
Denies that God has taken a child alongside any need for partner or protector, reinforcing divine independence.
Moses' admission of past error has no material connection to the focus.
Taking a particular friend is unrelated to the attribution of a child to God.
The refusal to prostrate to the Merciful concerns recognition of His name, not the child claim.
The recording of a boast about wealth and children is nearby context but does not explain 19:92.
Directly identifies those who say that God has taken a child as the object of warning.
Denies that the sovereign Creator has taken a child and links that denial to exclusive dominion.
The crowd around God's servant does not clarify the incompatibility of divine sonship.
Taking God as a trustee is a different relation from taking a child.
The denial that creatures should take protectors besides God offers only a broad boundary against unauthorized relations.
Israel's scripture and prophethood do not contribute to the focus.
Taking the calf as an object of worship is unrelated to the claim that the Merciful takes a child.
The Merciful's name and Satan's disobedience provide only distant same-surah background.
The future consequences of ridicule do not clarify divine sonship.
The calf episode is not a useful neighbour for the focus.
The Merciful's true dominion supports divine transcendence but does not address child attribution directly.
Jesus' declaration of servanthood and goodness to his mother completes the immediate human identity context.
Rejects the claim that God has taken a child and affirms that all things belong to Him.
The Prophet's request for no reward has no relevant connection.
The dispute over campaign participation is unrelated to the focus.
Military precautions have no material connection to divine sonship.
The ordered courses of celestial bodies do not clarify the focus.
The address to disbelievers does not supply a specific connection.
Using oaths as a shield is unrelated to the focus.
Human willing under God's will does not address taking a child.
The judgment scene offers no focused contribution to divine sonship.
The calf worshipers' fabrication is too remote from the specific offspring claim.
Directly rejects the claim that the Merciful has taken a child by defining the alleged beings as honored servants.
Moses' fear of being denied is unrelated to the focus.
Explicitly denies that the exalted Lord has taken either a spouse or a child.
The Prophet's trustworthiness regarding the unseen does not clarify divine sonship.
Moses being raised as a child uses ordinary human upbringing, not the focus's theological claim.
Challenges the attribution of daughters to God from among His creatures, a related critique of invented divine genealogy.
Creation for worship supports the creature-Creator distinction but is not a direct sonship parallel.
Parent-and-child language here is too general to illuminate divine offspring.
Its absolute denial that God begets or is begotten is a core parallel to 19:92.
Pharaoh's disobedience and punishment are unrelated to the focus.
The divine name the Merciful alone does not add a substantive connection.
Taking protectors besides God is a different relation from taking a child.
Critiques a false likeness assigned to the Merciful, supporting the rejection of invented filial descriptions.
Taking desire as a god does not clarify the focus.
Mary's vow to the Merciful is part of the immediate narrative that precedes the anti-sonship correction.
The prohibition on taking disbelievers as allies is unrelated to divine offspring.
Universal humbling before the Merciful supplies distant support for His exclusive transcendence.
Jesus disavows commanding worship of himself and his mother, directly extending the correction of false elevation.
The paired divine names do not by themselves clarify the claim rejected in 19:92.
The nearby taking of false gods concerns misplaced worship, not the Merciful taking a child.
Denies that God has taken a child and shows that competing divine claims would destroy coherent sovereignty.
Taking desire as a god is unrelated to the focus.
Following Satan and altering creation do not clarify divine sonship.
Mocking a messenger has no focused connection.
Ordinary human adoption provides only a distant contrast to the divine relation denied in 19:92.
Children as a worldly trial do not illuminate divine offspring.
Taking peers for God is related to idolatry but not a useful neighbour for the child attribution.
Separating belief in God from His messengers offers only broad doctrinal background.
Taking disbelievers as allies is unrelated to the focus.
Taking intercessors is a different theological relation and does not clarify sonship.
The rejection of humans taking one another as lords reinforces exclusive worship, though not the specific child claim.
Taking weapons during prayer is unrelated to the focus.
Human adoption of Joseph supplies only a distant contrast to the divine taking denied here.
The claimed covenant with the Merciful is nearby context but does not explain divine sonship.
The oath by unseen things has no connection to the focus.
The claim of a covenant with the Merciful belongs to the nearby polemic but is not the child attribution itself.
Solomon's prayer for gratitude has no material connection.
Earthly kinship and children not benefiting on Judgment Day do not clarify divine sonship.
The prohibition on killing children is unrelated to the focus.
Taking protectors besides God does not illuminate the claim that He takes a child.
Dietary necessity and mercy are unrelated to the focus.
Wealth and children not availing against God do not clarify divine offspring.
Family members as possible enemies are unrelated to the focus.
Explicitly identifies the assertion that God gave birth as a lie.
The divine name Merciful occurs in a dietary ruling without a relevant sonship connection.
Disbelief in the Merciful gives only distant background for the focus.
The denial of claims about Jesus' killing is relevant Christological context, but does not itself address divine sonship.
Repentance and success do not clarify the focus.
Household etiquette and the phrase what is fitting are unrelated to divine sonship.
The oath by the moon has no material connection.
Jesus' cradle speech and miracles by God's permission reinforce his servantly, God-dependent identity.
The decree of death does not clarify the offspring attribution.
Marital rules and seeking what God has written do not contribute to the focus.
Household access and greetings are unrelated to divine sonship.
The instruction to preserve human paternal attribution offers only a distant genealogy-related contrast.
Condemns inventing sons and daughters for God without knowledge, directly exposing the false attribution rejected in 19:92.
God's command Be creates without progeny, directly explaining why taking a child is unfitting.
The Originator of the heavens and earth has no consort and created all things; this directly rules out His having a child.
Names the claims that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son and identifies them as imitative, false speech.
Treats the elevation of religious authorities and the Messiah as lords as a related form of over-attribution against exclusive divinity.
Critiques assigning daughters to God, a related fabrication of divine genealogy.
Exposes the false and self-serving descriptions people assign to God, including the offspring-attribution polemic's wider pattern.
Challenges the inconsistent claim that God chose daughters while His creatures are assigned sons, rejecting fabricated divine offspring.
Declares that neither claimants nor their forefathers have knowledge for saying that God has taken a child, calling it a grave utterance.
Jesus identifies himself as God's servant, furnishing the immediate counter-description to divine sonship.
Jesus declares God to be both his Lord and his hearers' Lord, reinforcing the Creator-servant distinction.
The dispute over Jesus immediately follows his self-description and frames the polemic answered by 19:92.
Characterizes the attribution of a child to the Merciful as an atrocious assertion.
Describes cosmic collapse as the response to the claim that the Merciful has taken a child.
States that every being comes to the Merciful only as a servant, directly excluding a filial relation.
Mary's chastity and the mother-son sign present Jesus' origin as a divine sign, not divine progeny.
Calls Mary and her son a sign, preserving their created, evidentiary status.
Challenges the claim that the Lord has daughters while the claimants have sons, directly contesting divine genealogy.
Rejects the assertion that angels are female, part of the same fabricated offspring account.
Challenges the allegation that God selected daughters over sons, continuing the direct rejection of invented filial attribution.
Critiques assigning God a part from among His servants, a related distortion of the Creator-servant distinction.
Rejects the designation of the angels, themselves servants of the Merciful, as female offspring.
Defines Jesus as a servant favored by God, directly countering a divine-son reading of his identity.
Challenges the unequal assignment of male children to claimants and female children to God, exposing the incoherence of the attribution.
Condemns naming angels with female names, a related false description of beings associated with God.
The annunciation identifies Jesus as the Messiah, son of Mary, establishing the human maternal identity at issue in the passage.
Jesus speaking in the cradle directly parallels the servant speech in Surah Maryam that precedes 19:92.
God creates as He wills by the command Be, explaining Jesus' extraordinary origin without a divine offspring relation.
Jesus' life-giving signs occur only by God's permission, preserving the distinction between servant and Creator.
God's address to Jesus concerning death and raising gives related Quranic context for his created and dependent status.
The comparison of Jesus with Adam directly rejects the inference that unusual creation establishes divine sonship.
Names Jesus as God's messenger and word while explicitly forbidding the claim that God has a child.
States that the Messiah does not disdain being a servant of God, directly reinforcing 19:93's servant identity.
Rejects identifying the Messiah, son of Mary, with God and affirms God's power over him and his mother.
Rejects worship of the Messiah, son of Mary, directly guarding against his deification.
Rejects triune formulations and reasserts the singular God, a close doctrinal boundary for the focus.
Describes the Messiah and his mother as mortal recipients of food, directly supporting a non-divine reading.
Jesus' testimony that God took him after his earthly mission reinforces his status as God's servant and witness.
Mary's chastity and reception of God's words provide a further Quranic account of Jesus' miraculous but created origin.
